title: How Earthworms Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss earthworms: Charles Darwin's 39-year study and his 1881 book on worms, earthworm size and abundance (up to 22 ft South African record, Australian Gippsland giant), North American earthworms as recent invasive immigrants from Europe and Asia after the last ice age, the three ecological classes (epigeic, endogeic, anecic), their digestion and gizzard grit, nitrogen-rich castings used in composting, five aortic arches and skin breathing, light-sensing skin and minimal brain, regeneration after cutting, simultaneous hermaphroditism and cocoon reproduction, lifespan, estivation, soil preferences, and ecological harms of invasive worms to forest understory and litter layer. The episode closes with a listener email about a Sherpa student and a holiday note.
topics: The Formation of Vegetable Mold through the Action of Worms

segments.title: Opening banter and Darwin's worm book
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode, then discuss Darwin's 39 years studying earthworms and his book on worm action, which sold well in the nineteenth century.
topics: The Formation of Vegetable Mold through the Action of Worms

segments.title: Earthworm research history and giant worms
segments.summary: Darwin's ideas were accepted for decades, leaving earthworm research neglected; some worms thought extinct reappeared, such as the Giant Palouse earthworm. Worm sizes range from about a centimeter to nine feet or more, with a 22-foot South African record.

segments.title: Earthworm abundance and biomass
segments.summary: Per hectare there can be 500,000 to two million worms, with total wet biomass about ten times that of all other above-ground animals combined.

segments.title: Invasive earthworms in North America
segments.summary: Earthworms in northern North America above roughly 40 degrees latitude are recent immigrants from Europe and Asia that arrived in root balls of imported plants. Native worms likely retreated south during the glacial period, and forest ecosystems adapted to life without worms.

segments.title: Three ecological classes of earthworms
segments.summary: Earthworms are classified by where they live: epigeic worms in leaf litter (red wigglers), endogeic worms in topsoil (pale, light-colored), and anecic worms, the nightcrawlers that dig deep and forage above ground at night.

segments.title: Fishing with worms and personal anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck recounts a fishing story in which a hooked bream died, and says it made him quit fishing with worms.

segments.title: Segmentation and movement
segments.summary: Earthworms are segmented, with about 100 to 150 rings, each controlled by separate muscles. Retractable bristles called setae anchor the front while the body contracts and extends to move forward.

segments.title: Earthworm digestion and nutrient cycling
segments.summary: Worms take in soil and organic matter, which passes through a crop and then a gizzard where pebbles grind food. Nutrients are absorbed in the intestine. Their castings contain nitrogen made available to plants, which is why worms are used in composting.

segments.title: Circulation, skin breathing, light sensing and brain
segments.summary: Earthworms have five aortic arches and breathe through their mucus-coated skin, which is why they drown in dry conditions. They have light-sensitive skin cells and a minimal brain, and can regenerate, usually the tail end more easily than the head.

segments.title: Pain in animals digression
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether worms feel pain, then move to David Foster Wallace's article on lobsters and historical views of lobster as food for the poor.

segments.title: Earthworm reproduction and cocoons
segments.summary: Earthworms are simultaneous hermaphrodites that exchange sperm lying head to tail inside a mucus tube. The clitellum produces a slime tube that collects eggs and fertilizes them, then forms a cocoon that holds several hatchlings. They can reproduce every seven to ten days.

segments.title: Lifespan, estivation, and soil preferences
segments.summary: Nightcrawlers live six to nine years, red wigglers two to five, and gray worms about one to two and a half. Estivation is a dormancy state that is more efficient than hibernation. Worms prefer certain temperatures and foods, such as clover over grass.

segments.title: Ecological benefits and harms of earthworms
segments.summary: Earthworms aerate soil, create macropores that help water drain, and produce castings. Darwin estimated castings could cover an acre. However, as invasive species they consume leaf litter faster than it accumulates, reducing duff, seedlings and understory plants, and affecting spiders and other fauna. Carbon release in North American studies contrasts with carbon locking in Vietnam and Malaysia.
